title: Radiograph faults & how to avoid them
blurb: Elongation, foreshortening, overlapped contacts, cone cut, cut-off apices, blurring, reversed receptors, panoramic positioning errors and processing faults: what causes each and how to prevent it.
question: A lower molar periapical comes back with the roots looking short and stubby, and the next bitewing has an unexposed white area along one edge. Later a panoramic shows a dark band across the upper tooth roots. What caused each fault, and what should be done differently before any retake?

teach.body: Most faults come from a handful of causes: the receptor in the wrong place, the beam at the wrong angle, the patient moving, a metal object left in, the wrong exposure, or a processing or handling error. Each faulty image may mean a retake, which doubles the patient's dose for that view. Learn to read the fault, name the cause and fix it before the next exposure, and you protect the patient and save time.

teach.caption: Holders with beam-aiming devices set both angles for you, which is why they cut retakes so effectively.

An unexposed white area along the left of the image, where the beam missed part of the receptor, so the most posterior tooth can't be fully assessed. Fix: line the aiming ring and collimator up with the holder.

teach.h: Receptor position and other intraoral faults
teach.body: If the root tips are missing, the receptor wasn't placed far enough into the mouth, so place it deeper. If the back of the most posterior tooth is cut off, the receptor was too far forward (mesial), so move it further back. A reversed film looks pale with the lead foil pattern; a reversed phosphor plate may show the outline of its backing and comes out the wrong way round; a reversed sensor shows its circuitry. Dentures or appliances left in show as white shapes over the area of interest.

teach.caption: The whole panoramic image is blurred because the patient moved during the scan. The bright white circle on the right is an earring that should have been removed.

A dark (radiolucent) band over the roots of the upper teeth. The air space between the tongue and the palate hides the upper apices. Fix: ask the patient to swallow and keep the tongue pressed to the roof of the mouth.

head: Appearance
Likely cause
rows: Over-exposed, or developer too hot, long or strong
Under-exposed, or developer cold, short or exhausted
Fixer exhausted or fixing too short
Developer (black) or fixer (white) splashed on film

teach.text: Foreshortened = Fore-SHORT-ened = SHORT roots = beam too STEEP. Elongated = LONG roots = beam too SHALLOW. And only retake when the fault stops the image answering the clinical question, after fixing the cause.

items: Too much vertical angle = foreshortening; too little = elongation; wrong horizontal angle = overlapped contacts.
Cone cut = beam not centred on the receptor; apices cut off = receptor not placed deep enough.
DPT: tongue down = dark band over upper roots; movement = blur; metal = white artefacts.
Retake only when diagnosis is compromised, after correcting the cause. Holders and good technique prevent most faults.

summary: You can now recognise the common intraoral, panoramic, exposure and processing faults, name the cause of each, explain how to correct it, and decide when a retake is genuinely needed.

A.q: A periapical of a lower molar shows the roots looking short and stubby. What is the most likely cause?
A.why: Excessive vertical angulation projects the roots shorter than they are: foreshortening.

whyNot.0: Too little vertical angulation makes the roots look too long (elongation).
whyNot.1: Wrong horizontal angulation causes overlapped contacts, not short roots.
whyNot.3: Movement causes blurring rather than a change in root length.

A.q: A bitewing shows heavily overlapped contact points between the premolars. What should be corrected before retaking?
options: The vertical angulation of the beam
A.why: Overlapped contacts mean the beam wasn't aimed through the contact points; correct the horizontal angle.

whyNot.0: Vertical angle errors change root length, not contact overlap.
whyNot.2: Exposure time affects density, not overlap.
whyNot.3: Processing affects density or stains, not tooth overlap.

A.q: A panoramic radiograph shows a dark band across the apices of the upper teeth. What is the most likely cause?
options: Chin tipped too far up in the machine
A.why: If the tongue isn't pressed to the palate, the air space above it shows as a radiolucent band over the upper roots.

whyNot.0: Earrings show as white artefacts, not a dark band.
whyNot.1: A raised chin flattens the occlusal plane and puts the palate over the upper roots, rather than a dark air band.
whyNot.2: Movement causes general blurring, not a defined dark band.

B.q: A radiograph has an unexposed white area with a sharp edge along one side. What is this fault?
B.why: A cone cut happens when the beam isn't centred on the receptor, leaving part of it unexposed.

whyNot.1: Elongation makes roots look too long; it doesn't leave an unexposed area.
whyNot.2: Double exposure shows two superimposed images.
whyNot.3: A reversed film is pale overall with the foil pattern.

B.q: A lower molar periapical shows the crowns clearly but the root tips are missing. What is the best correction?
B.why: Missing apices mean the receptor wasn't placed far enough into the mouth; position it deeper so the apices are included.

whyNot.0: More exposure won't capture an area that isn't on the receptor.
whyNot.2: A round collimator increases dose and doesn't fix receptor position.
whyNot.3: Swallowing relates to tongue position for a DPT, not periapical coverage.

B.q: A whole panoramic image is generally blurred. What should be done before repeating it?
B.why: General blurring is caused by movement; explain the procedure, use the head supports and ask the patient to stay still until the machine stops.

whyNot.0: More exposure doesn't prevent movement and adds dose.
whyNot.1: A collar doesn't stop movement and can block the image.
whyNot.3: Tilting the chin down causes its own fault (an exaggerated smile).

C.q: A film radiograph has a green, opaque tinge after processing. What is the most likely cause?
C.why: Exhausted fixer, or too short a fixing time, leaves a green, opaque tinge.

whyNot.1: Hot developer makes the image too dark.
whyNot.2: Over-exposure gives a dark image, not a green tinge.

C.q: A periapical shows the roots of a lower molar looking unusually long and stretched. What caused this?
options: Wrong horizontal angulation of the beam
C.why: Insufficient vertical angulation projects the roots longer than they are: elongation.

whyNot.0: Too much vertical angulation shortens the roots (foreshortening).
whyNot.1: Receptor depth affects whether apices are included, not root length.
whyNot.3: Horizontal angle errors cause overlapped contacts.

C.q: Under IR(ME)R principles, when is a retake justified?
options: When the image is slightly pale
To keep a spare copy on file
C.why: A retake is only justified when the fault means the image can't answer the clinical question, and only after the cause is corrected.

whyNot.0: A slightly pale image that is still diagnostic should not be repeated.
whyNot.2: Patient request alone doesn't justify extra dose.
whyNot.3: Spare images are never a justification for exposure.

reteach.title: Torch and shadow puppet
reteach.question: If you shine a torch at your hand to make a shadow on the wall, what happens to the shadow when you change the torch angle or move?

blocks.body: Shine the torch straight down from high above and your hand's shadow gets short and squat: that's foreshortening, from too steep a beam. Hold the torch low and the shadow stretches long: elongation, from too shallow a beam. Shine from the side and your fingers overlap: overlapped contacts, from the wrong horizontal angle. Point the torch slightly off the wall and part of the wall stays dark: on a radiograph that's a white cone cut. And if your hand moves, the shadow smudges: blurring.

blocks.text: Fix the cause first, then retake once. A second retake with the same mistake doubles the dose again for nothing.

explain.body: Too steep (too much vertical angle) and the roots look short: foreshortening. Too shallow (too little) and the roots look long: elongation. A holder with a beam-aiming device prevents both.

test.q: Which fault results from excessive vertical angulation of the beam?
test.why: Too much vertical angulation shortens the image of the tooth: foreshortening.

whyNot.0: Elongation comes from too little vertical angulation.
whyNot.1: Cone cut comes from a beam not centred on the receptor.
whyNot.2: Overlapped contacts come from the wrong horizontal angle.

explain.body: If the beam isn't aimed through the contact points, neighbouring teeth overlap. If the beam isn't centred on the receptor, part of it is unexposed: a white cone cut. Align the aiming ring and collimator with the holder.

explain.caption: Cone cut: the white area at the left was never exposed.

options: The beam not centred on the receptor
The receptor placed back to front
test.why: If the beam is misaligned with the receptor, part of the receptor receives no X-rays and appears white.

whyNot.2: Exhausted developer gives a pale image overall.
whyNot.3: A reversed receptor gives a pale image or shows its backing, not a sharp-edged unexposed area.

explain.body: Remove metal, stand straight, bite in the groove, Frankfort plane horizontal, midline vertical, tongue to palate, keep still. Each mistake has its own signature on the image.

explain.caption: Dark band over the upper roots: tongue not on the palate.

test.q: A DPT shows an exaggerated 'smile' curve and the lower incisor apices cut off. What was wrong?
test.why: With the chin tipped down, the occlusal plane curves into an exaggerated smile and the lower incisor apices can be cut off.

whyNot.0: A raised chin gives a flat or reversed smile.
whyNot.1: A turned head makes teeth wider on one side.
whyNot.3: Tongue position causes a dark band over the upper roots.

explain.body: Over-exposure or hot, long or strong developer: dark. Under-exposure or cold, short or exhausted developer: pale. Exhausted fixer: green tinge. Poor washing: brown later. Fixer splashes white, developer splashes black.

test.q: A film is pale and lacks contrast, although the exposure settings were correct. What is the most likely processing cause?
test.why: Exhausted, cold or short development under-develops the film, leaving it pale with poor contrast.

whyNot.1: Fixer splashes leave white marks, not a uniformly pale image.
whyNot.2: Hot developer makes the image too dark.
whyNot.3: Longer washing removes leftover chemicals; it doesn't make the image pale.
